cases.title: Fasting glucose at baseline, 6 weeks and 12 weeks of a walking program
cases.context: In a clinical trial, fasting plasma glucose (the concentration of glucose in the blood after an overnight fast) was measured in milligrams per deciliter (mg/dL) in 5 patients with prediabetes (blood glucose above the normal range but below the range for diabetes). Each patient was measured at baseline, after 6 weeks and after 12 weeks of a supervised walking program. The data are listed in the table below.
tasks: Is there a difference in fasting plasma glucose over time? Assume that any quantities of interest are Normally distributed. (Note: If a difference exists, do not identify which times are different.)
Make sure to show your intermediate calculations. DO NOT use R.

hypotheses.alternative: H_A:\text{not all three population means are equal}
hypotheses.nullWords: There is no difference in mean fasting plasma glucose at baseline, after 6 weeks and after 12 weeks of the walking program.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: Mean fasting plasma glucose differs at one or more of the three times.

cases.symbols: \(x_{ts}\) (observation for treatment \(t\), subject \(s\)), \(m\) (number of treatments), \(n\) (number of subjects), \(\bar S_s\) (subject mean), \(\bar T_t\) (treatment mean), \(\bar X\) (grand mean), \(SS\) (sum of squares), \(DF\) (degrees of freedom), \(MS\) (mean square), \(F\) (F statistic).

steps.title: State the procedure and design
steps.words: The same 5 patients are measured at all 3 times, so the observations are repeated measures on the same subjects. Repeated measures ANOVA is the procedure. It removes the large differences in glucose between patients from the error term before comparing the times.

steps.title: State the hypotheses
steps.words: There is no difference in mean fasting plasma glucose at baseline, after 6 weeks and after 12 weeks of the walking program. Mean fasting plasma glucose differs at one or more of the three times.

steps.title: Calculate each subject mean
steps.words: Average each patient across all 3 times. Each row of the table gives one subject mean.

steps.title: Calculate the treatment means and the grand mean
steps.words: Average each column over the 5 patients. The grand mean is the mean of all 15 observations, which equals the mean of the treatment means.

steps.title: Calculate the within-subjects sum of squares
steps.words: Each patient is compared only with its own mean, so differences between patients never enter this sum. It holds the treatment effect plus residual scatter.

steps.title: Calculate the treatment sum of squares
steps.words: Multiply by n because each treatment mean involves n subjects.

steps.title: Calculate the residual sum of squares
steps.words: The residual is the within-subject variation that the treatment means do not explain.

steps.title: Find the degrees of freedom and mean squares
steps.words: Each sum of squares is divided by its own degrees of freedom to give a variance estimate.

steps.title: Calculate the F statistic
steps.words: Treatment variance is compared with residual variance. Values near 1 or below are what equal treatment means produce.

steps.title: Find the critical value
steps.words: Start with α = 0.05. Open F_table.pdf, PDF page 1. Use numerator column ν_n=2 and denominator row ν_d=8. The lightface entry 4.46 is the 0.05 cutoff and the boldface entry 8.65 is the 0.01 cutoff. Swapping the two df selects a different, wrong cell.

steps.title: Make the decision
steps.words: F is above both the 0.05 and the 0.01 cutoffs, so reject the null hypothesis with P < 0.01.

cases.conclusion: F = 58.515 with 2 and 8 degrees of freedom exceeds F_0.01(2,8) = 8.65. Reject H0, P < 0.01. There is a difference in mean fasting plasma glucose among baseline, 6 weeks and 12 weeks of the walking program. Holm-corrected pairwise t tests are then needed to locate the difference.

cases.title: Holm-corrected comparisons of fasting glucose times
cases.context: In a clinical trial, fasting plasma glucose (the concentration of glucose in the blood after an overnight fast) was measured in the same 5 patients with prediabetes at baseline, after 6 weeks and after 12 weeks of a supervised walking program. A repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed on the data, resulting in the conclusion that there is a difference in fasting plasma glucose among the three times (F = 58.515, P < 0.01). From the ANOVA, the treatment means were 119.6, 114.4 and 108.2 milligrams per deciliter (mg/dL) at baseline, 6 weeks and 12 weeks (each mean is based on n = 5 patients), and the residual mean square was MS_res = 2.783333 with DF_res = 8 residual degrees of freedom.
tasks: Perform the appropriate form of multiple pairwise comparisons, testing every time against every other time, using the Holm correction to determine which of the three times differ from one another. Use the relevant information from the ANOVA results to do your calculations.

Present your final/overall conclusion on which times are different from one another (and which times are not different) using an overall level of significance of 0.05. Please state how you reached your conclusions.

hypotheses.nullWords: For the pair being compared, there is no difference in mean fasting plasma glucose between the two times.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: For that pair, mean fasting plasma glucose differs between the two times.

cases.symbols: \(\bar T_i\) (treatment mean), \(MS_{res}\) (residual mean square), \(n\) (number of subjects), \(DF_{res}\) (residual degrees of freedom), \(k\) (number of pairwise comparisons), \(\alpha_j\) (Holm level for the \(j\)th comparison), \(\alpha_T\) (overall level).

steps.title: State the procedure
steps.words: The overall F test rejected, so pairwise t tests with the Holm correction locate the differences. The repeated-measures version uses MS_res in the standard error and DF_res for the t table.

steps.title: State the hypotheses for each pair
steps.words: For the pair being compared, there is no difference in mean fasting plasma glucose between the two times. For that pair, mean fasting plasma glucose differs between the two times.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of a difference
steps.words: The same standard error serves every pair because every treatment mean is based on the same n subjects.

steps.title: Calculate every pairwise t statistic
steps.words: Keep the subtraction order. The sign only gives the direction, and the ranking uses |t|.

steps.title: Order by |t| and set the Holm levels
steps.words: The largest |t| is tested at the strictest level. Testing stops at the first comparison that is not significant.

steps.title: Comparison 1: Baseline vs 12 weeks
steps.words: The 0.0167 column is not printed. In t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 8, the printed neighbors are the 0.02 column (2.896) and the 0.01 column (3.355). Use the stricter 0.01 column, 3.355, because a statistic beyond it is significant at 0.0167 as well. |t| = 10.804 > 3.355, so the Baseline and 12 weeks means differ (P<0.001 before adjustment).

steps.title: Comparison 2: 6 weeks vs 12 weeks
steps.words: The 0.025 column is not printed. In t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 8, the printed neighbors are the 0.05 column (2.306) and the 0.02 column (2.896). Use the stricter 0.02 column, 2.896, because a statistic beyond it is significant at 0.025 as well. |t| = 5.876 > 2.896, so the 6 weeks and 12 weeks means differ (P<0.001 before adjustment).

steps.title: Comparison 3: Baseline vs 6 weeks
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 8, combined two-tail 0.05 column. The entry is 2.306. |t| = 4.928 > 2.306, so the Baseline and 6 weeks means differ (0.001<P<0.002 before adjustment).

cases.conclusion: All three pairs differ at the Holm-corrected levels. Mean fasting plasma glucose is lower at 12 weeks than at baseline (t = 10.804), lower at 12 weeks than at 6 weeks (t = 5.876) and lower at 6 weeks than at baseline (t = 4.928).

cases.title: Anemia before and after iron supplementation
cases.context: Researchers interested in iron supplements did a study to evaluate anemia (a hemoglobin concentration below 12 grams per deciliter, g/dL) in young women. Each of 34 women was tested for anemia before and again after 3 months of taking an oral iron tablet every day. Of the 21 women with anemia before supplementation, 8 still had anemia after and 13 did not. Of the 13 women without anemia before, 2 had anemia after and 11 did not.
tasks: Based on the recorded data, is there evidence that the proportion of women with anemia is different before and after iron supplementation?

Provide your result in a single complete sentence that would convey your conclusion in a way that could be understood by a non-expert in statistics or medicine (e.g., a typical reader of a local newspaper).

hypotheses.nullWords: Iron supplementation has no effect on anemia status, so a woman whose status changes is equally likely to change from anemia to no anemia as from no anemia to anemia.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The two directions of change are not equally likely, so the proportion of women with anemia differs before and after supplementation.

cases.symbols: \(a,d\) (subjects with the same result both times), \(b,c\) (subjects whose result changes), \(E\) (expected number in each change cell), \(\chi^2\) (McNemar chi-square), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom).

steps.title: State the procedure
steps.words: Each woman is classified twice, before and after supplementation, so the two classifications are paired nominal data. This design is analogous to the paired t test, and McNemar's test is the procedure.

steps.title: State the hypotheses
steps.words: Iron supplementation has no effect on anemia status, so a woman whose status changes is equally likely to change from anemia to no anemia as from no anemia to anemia. The two directions of change are not equally likely, so the proportion of women with anemia differs before and after supplementation.

steps.title: Show why the independent chi-square is wrong here
steps.words: Treating the before and after results as independent samples gives chi-square = 1.051, which would wrongly suggest no change. The rows and columns describe the same women, so they are not independent, and this test is not valid for the design.

steps.title: Identify the subjects who change
steps.words: Only discordant subjects carry information about a change. Here b counts women with anemia before and none after and c counts women without anemia before and with anemia after. The concordant cells a = 8 and d = 11 do not enter the statistic.

steps.title: Calculate the expected number in each change cell
steps.words: If the null hypothesis is true, the changes split evenly in the two directions.

steps.title: Calculate the McNemar chi-square with Yates correction
steps.words: Subtract one half from each absolute difference before squaring because the table is 2 x 2 (Yates correction).

steps.title: Find the critical value
steps.words: Start with α = 0.05. Open Chi_Squared_Table2.pdf, PDF page 1. Row df = 1, column χ².050 gives 3.841. The same row gives 2.706 in the .100 column, 5.024 in the .025 column, 6.635 in the .010 column and 7.879 in the .005 column for a P range.

steps.title: Make the decision
steps.words: Reject the null hypothesis. The statistic lies between two printed cutoffs, so 0.005 < P < 0.01.

cases.conclusion: McNemar chi-square = 6.6667 with 1 df exceeds chi-square_0.01(1) = 6.635 but not chi-square_0.005(1) = 7.879. Reject H0, 0.005 < P < 0.01. There is a difference in the proportion of women with anemia before and after iron supplementation. Of the 15 women who changed, 13 went from anemia to no anemia. In plain words, fewer of the young women in this study were anemic after three months of daily iron tablets than before.

cases.title: Hypertension before and after a low-sodium diet
cases.context: In a study looking at dietary salt and blood pressure, 26 adults were classified as hypertensive (systolic blood pressure of 140 millimeters of mercury, mmHg, or higher) or not hypertensive. Each adult was evaluated before and again after 8 weeks of a low-sodium diet. Of the 16 adults who were hypertensive before the diet, 9 were still hypertensive after and 7 were not. Of the 10 adults who were not hypertensive before, 3 were hypertensive after and 7 were not.
tasks: Based on the recorded data, is there evidence that the proportion of adults with hypertension is different before and after the low-sodium diet?

Provide your result in a single complete sentence that would convey your conclusion in a way that could be understood by a non-expert in statistics or medicine (e.g., a typical reader of a local newspaper).

hypotheses.nullWords: The diet has no effect on hypertension status, so an adult whose status changes is equally likely to change from hypertensive to not hypertensive as the other way.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The two directions of change are not equally likely, so the proportion of adults with hypertension differs before and after the diet.

cases.symbols: \(a,d\) (subjects with the same result both times), \(b,c\) (subjects whose result changes), \(E\) (expected number in each change cell), \(\chi^2\) (McNemar chi-square), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom).

steps.title: State the procedure
steps.words: Each adult is classified twice, before and after the diet, so the two classifications are paired nominal data. This design is analogous to the paired t test, and McNemar's test is the procedure.

steps.title: State the hypotheses
steps.words: The diet has no effect on hypertension status, so an adult whose status changes is equally likely to change from hypertensive to not hypertensive as the other way. The two directions of change are not equally likely, so the proportion of adults with hypertension differs before and after the diet.

steps.title: Show why the independent chi-square is wrong here
steps.words: Treating the before and after results as independent samples gives chi-square = 0.813. This value answers a different question (whether the after result is related to the before result) and it is not used. The rows and columns describe the same adults, so they are not independent, and this test is not valid for the design.

steps.title: Identify the subjects who change
steps.words: Only discordant subjects carry information about a change. Here b counts adults hypertensive before and not after and c counts adults not hypertensive before and hypertensive after. The concordant cells a = 9 and d = 7 do not enter the statistic.

steps.title: Calculate the expected number in each change cell
steps.words: If the null hypothesis is true, the changes split evenly in the two directions.

steps.title: Calculate the McNemar chi-square with Yates correction
steps.words: Subtract one half from each absolute difference before squaring because the table is 2 x 2 (Yates correction).

steps.title: Find the critical value
steps.words: Start with α = 0.05. Open Chi_Squared_Table2.pdf, PDF page 1. Row df = 1, column χ².050 gives 3.841. The same row gives 2.706 in the .100 column, 5.024 in the .025 column, 6.635 in the .010 column and 7.879 in the .005 column for a P range.

steps.title: Make the decision
steps.words: Do not reject the null hypothesis because the statistic is below the 0.05 cutoff and even below the .100 cutoff (P > 0.10).

cases.conclusion: McNemar chi-square = 0.9 with 1 df is below chi-square_0.05(1) = 3.841 and also below chi-square_0.10(1) = 2.706. Do not reject H0 (P > 0.10). There is no evidence of a difference in the proportion of adults with hypertension before and after the low-sodium diet, even though 7 adults improved and 3 got worse. In plain words, this small study could not show that the diet changed how many adults had high blood pressure.

cases.title: Heart muscle injury by a point-of-care troponin test and a laboratory assay
cases.context: A study was reported concerning a point-of-care troponin test (a bedside blood test for heart muscle injury that gives a result in about 15 minutes). Each of 40 patients with chest pain in an emergency department was classified as positive or negative for heart muscle injury by the point-of-care test and by a high-sensitivity troponin assay run in the central laboratory. Of the 10 patients called positive by the point-of-care test, 9 were positive and 1 was negative by the laboratory assay. Of the 30 patients called negative by the point-of-care test, 13 were positive and 17 were negative by the laboratory assay.
tasks: Is there a difference between the point-of-care test and the laboratory assay in the proportion of patients classified as positive? Use a chi-square test.
Please state how you reached your conclusions.

hypotheses.nullWords: The point-of-care test and the laboratory assay have the same probability of calling a patient positive, so patients on whom they disagree are equally likely to be positive by the point-of-care test only as by the laboratory assay only.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The two methods differ in how often they call a patient positive for heart muscle injury.

steps.title: State the procedure
steps.words: Both methods classify the same 40 patients, so the results are paired nominal data. McNemar's test compares two diagnostic procedures applied to the same people.

steps.title: State the hypotheses
steps.words: The point-of-care test and the laboratory assay have the same probability of calling a patient positive, so patients on whom they disagree are equally likely to be positive by the point-of-care test only as by the laboratory assay only. The two methods differ in how often they call a patient positive for heart muscle injury.

steps.title: Identify the subjects who change
steps.words: Only discordant subjects carry information about a difference. Here b counts patients called positive by the point-of-care test but negative by the laboratory assay and c counts patients called negative by the point-of-care test but positive by the laboratory assay. The concordant cells a = 9 and d = 17 do not enter the statistic.

steps.title: Calculate the expected number in each change cell
steps.words: If the null hypothesis is true, the changes split evenly in the two directions.

steps.title: Calculate the McNemar chi-square with Yates correction
steps.words: Subtract one half from each absolute difference before squaring because the table is 2 x 2 (Yates correction).

steps.title: Find the critical value
steps.words: Start with α = 0.05. Open Chi_Squared_Table2.pdf, PDF page 1. Row df = 1, column χ².050 gives 3.841. The same row gives 2.706 in the .100 column, 5.024 in the .025 column, 6.635 in the .010 column and 7.879 in the .005 column for a P range.

steps.title: Make the decision
steps.words: Reject the null hypothesis. The statistic is above even the .005 cutoff, so P < 0.005.

cases.conclusion: McNemar chi-square = 8.6429 with 1 df exceeds chi-square_0.005(1) = 7.879. Reject H0, P < 0.005. There is a difference between the two methods. The laboratory assay calls patients positive more often than the point-of-care test does (13 patients positive by the laboratory assay only against 1 positive by the point-of-care test only).

cases.title: Atrial fibrillation by a smartwatch and by a cardiologist
cases.context: In a study looking at wearable heart rhythm monitoring, 30 adults wore a smartwatch with a single-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) sensor and a Holter monitor (a portable recorder of the full ECG) for 24 hours. Each adult was classified as positive or negative for atrial fibrillation (AF, an irregular and often fast heart rhythm) by the smartwatch algorithm and by a cardiologist reading the Holter recording. Of the 16 adults called positive by the smartwatch, 6 were positive and 10 were negative by the cardiologist. Of the 14 adults called negative by the smartwatch, 3 were positive and 11 were negative by the cardiologist.
tasks: Is there a difference between the smartwatch and the cardiologist in the proportion of adults classified as having AF? Use a chi-square test.
Please state how you reached your conclusions.

steps.words: Only discordant subjects carry information about a difference. steps.words: Start with α = 0.05. Open Chi_Squared_Table2.pdf, PDF page 1. Row df = 1, column χ².050 gives 3.841. The same row gives 2.706 in the .100 column, 5.024 in the .025 column, 6.635 in the .010 column and 7.879 in the .005 column for a P range.

steps.words: Do not reject the null hypothesis because the statistic is below the 0.05 cutoff. It lies between the .100 and .050 cutoffs, so 0.05 < P < 0.10.

There is no evidence of a difference between the smartwatch and the cardiologist in how often adults are classified as having AF, even though the smartwatch alone called 10 adults positive and the cardiologist alone called 3.
